subject: biology
title: Planning your practical investigation and poster

scenes.heading: Planning your investigation and poster
scenes.sub: Think and work like a real biologist
scenes.say: In Unit 4 you design your own investigation and present it as a scientific poster. Careful planning is the single biggest factor in a good result. Let's walk through every stage.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Testing which charger fills your phone fastest, fairly
scenes.science: Change one variable, measure another, keep the rest the same
scenes.breaks: you test the same phone each time, but living material varies naturally, so biology usually needs more replicates.
scenes.say: Say you're testing whether a new charger is faster. The charger is the independent variable. Battery gained in thirty minutes is the dependent variable. Same phone, same starting level: those are controlled variables. An unplugged phone is a negative control. And repeat each test, because one result could be a fluke.
scenes.caption: Say you're testing whether a new charger is faster. The charger is the independent variable. Battery gained in 30 minutes is the dependent variable. Same phone, same starting level: those are controlled variables. An unplugged phone is a negative control. And repeat each test, because one result could be a fluke.

scenes.heading: Planning steps
steps: Change one variable; control the rest
At least three replicates per level
scenes.say: Start with a focused, testable research question. Write a hypothesis: if, then, because. Change only one independent variable and control the rest. Do at least three replicates at each level. And complete a risk assessment and think about ethics before you start. Results only support a hypothesis, they never prove it.

scenes.heading: Don't mix these up
scenes.say: Controlled variables are the things you keep the same, like the volume of hydrogen peroxide. A control is a set-up you compare against, like boiled potato as a negative control. One is a rule, the other is a test tube.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Yeast CO₂ is measured at 0–8% sucrose in 10 min at 30 °C. The thermometer reads 2 °C high. What kind of error?
lines: Every trial is wrong by the same amount
Fix: calibrate or replace the thermometer
scenes.say: A student measures carbon dioxide from yeast at different sucrose levels. The thermometer reads two degrees too high. Every trial is off by the same amount, so it's a systematic error. It reduces accuracy. Fix the equipment, because more repeats won't help.

scenes.heading: Random vs systematic error
points: Fix random: more replicates, take a mean
scenes.say: Random errors are unpredictable, like reading a syringe by eye. They reduce precision, and more replicates with averaging help. Systematic errors shift everything the same way and reduce accuracy.

scenes.heading: Your poster
scenes.say: Your poster is the highlights package. Tim Reads Daily, Carefully Reviewing: title, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion, references. Keep it visual. Your logbook is the full replay, with every plan and raw reading.

points: One independent variable; control the rest
scenes.say: Quick recap. Ask a focused question and write a testable hypothesis. Change one variable, control the rest, and repeat. Know your errors. And make your poster clear and honest. Now try the practice questions!
